language.name: French
language.variety: Standard French · formal vous · minimal production grammar
features: A regular statement keeps subject + verb + complement; use est-ce que to ask questions.
Use passé composé (auxiliary + participle) for past events; short states use imparfait.
Use aller + infinitive for a near-future plan.
Use ne/n’ ... pas around the finite verb group for negative statements.
The printed masculine adjective and movement participles change agreement for a feminine speaker.

lessons.title: Begin a conversation
lessons.goal: Greet someone, be polite, and end an exchange
lessons.introduction: Keep a handful of social formulas as complete units. The rest of the manual builds productive sentences.

notes.recipe: Bonjour. / Merci. / Excusez-moi.
notes.explanation: Memorize basic social conventions, but build productive sentences from subjects, verbs and complements.
notes.detail: Vous is the formal you. Our production subset uses it consistently for polite communication, even with one person.
notes.caution: Some social formulas do not have a fully productive derivation. That is a documented exception, not the main learning method.

lessons.title: People and simple states
lessons.goal: Say who is doing something and describe a current state
lessons.introduction: Change the subject or quality while keeping the same sentence skeleton.

notes.recipe: Je / vous / nous / il + verb + complement.
notes.explanation: French statements usually keep the subject explicitly before a conjugated verb.
notes.detail: The core être forms are je suis, vous êtes, nous sommes, il est. French adjectives may agree in gender and number. The default model prints masculine forms for je and singular formal vous.
notes.caution: A feminine speaker normally adds -e to adjectives such as fatigué → fatiguée. Do not treat one default form as universal.

lessons.title: Needs and possessions
lessons.goal: Communicate everyday needs and what you have
lessons.introduction: Change the object, not the entire sentence. Learn the short noun phrase together with its article.

notes.recipe: J’ai besoin de ... / J’ai ... / Je voudrais ...
notes.explanation: Needing something uses avoir besoin de. Wanting something politely uses je voudrais.
notes.detail: For count nouns, un/une depends on grammatical gender: un billet, une chambre. For mass nouns, French often uses du/de la/de l’, such as de l’eau. Deux + plural removes the article.
notes.caution: The de in avoir besoin de changes with the following sound: besoin d’un billet, besoin d’eau.

lessons.title: Ask simple questions
lessons.goal: Ask for confirmation, locations, and prices
lessons.introduction: A question changes sentence structure. It should not require learning a separate phrase for every verb.

notes.recipe: Est-ce que + ordinary statement + ?
notes.explanation: Instead of learning several inversion patterns, turn a statement into a question with est-ce que.
notes.detail: Où est ... ? asks for a place, and Combien coûte ... ? asks for price. These question forms can be reused with many nouns.
notes.caution: In ordinary writing a space normally precedes the French question mark.

examples.target: Est-ce que vous avez du temps ?
Est-ce que vous avez un rendez-vous ?
Est-ce que vous avez une question ?

examples.english: How much does a coffee cost?
How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a book cost?

lessons.title: Say what is not true
lessons.goal: Refuse, correct information, and say what you lack
lessons.introduction: Negation is a reusable operator over a clause; noun and verb negation differ between languages.

notes.recipe: ne/n’ + finite verb + pas
notes.explanation: Written French negation surrounds the finite verb group. The same rule works with present, past auxiliaries and future helpers.
notes.detail: Use n’ before a vowel: je n’ai pas, but je ne comprends pas. In a simple negative possession, un billet becomes de billet.
notes.caution: Spoken French often drops ne, but the guide retains it for predictable standard written forms.

examples.english: I do not have a ticket.
I do not have an appointment.
I do not understand a question.
examples.target: Je ne comprends pas une question.

lessons.title: Get around
lessons.goal: Find destinations and describe movement
lessons.introduction: Destinations are semantic slots. A language determines the preposition and article for each place.

notes.recipe: Où est ... ? / Je vais ... / Je reste ...
notes.explanation: A destination is a distinct semantic slot; its article and preposition are handled by the language.
notes.detail: Common destinations are à la gare, à l’hôpital, au bureau and chez moi. For staying, use a location rather than a direction.
notes.caution: Do not translate English to as a single fixed French preposition.

lessons.title: Describe ordinary life
lessons.goal: Talk about working, eating, drinking, and learning
lessons.introduction: Reuse the present tense for common activities and the things that go with them.

notes.recipe: Je / vous / nous + present verb + object.
notes.explanation: Present tense handles routine actions. The realizer applies the correct conjugated form to the shared event.
notes.detail: French uses different forms for je, vous, nous and il. A compact first pass memorizes high-frequency forms like je travaille, vous travaillez, nous travaillons.
notes.caution: French present-tense spelling and pronunciation do not always correspond one-to-one.

lessons.title: Can, cannot, and requests
lessons.goal: Ask permission, offer help, and describe ability
lessons.introduction: Modal verbs attach to an action. The action stays an infinitive in many languages.

notes.recipe: Je peux + infinitive. / Est-ce que vous pouvez ... ?
notes.explanation: Pouvoir expresses ability or permission. The next action remains an infinitive.
notes.detail: For help, French uses object pronouns: pouvez-vous m’aider becomes est-ce que vous pouvez m’aider in our no-inversion profile.
notes.caution: With modal verbs the object pronoun goes just before the infinitive: je peux vous aider.

examples.target: Est-ce que vous pouvez m’aider, s’il vous plaît ?
Est-ce que vous pouvez nous aider, s’il vous plaît ?
Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
Est-ce que je peux payer en espèces ?

lessons.title: Want and have to
lessons.goal: Communicate obligations, desires, and basic plans
lessons.introduction: Ability, desire, and obligation differ in meaning but share a reusable modal construction.

notes.recipe: Je veux / je dois + infinitive.
notes.explanation: Vouloir expresses desire and devoir expresses an obligation. Both accept an infinitive action.
notes.detail: Je dois travailler and je veux aller both reuse the same finite-plus-infinitive structure.
notes.caution: Je voudrais is normally more courteous than je veux when asking for a product or service.

examples.english: I have to go to the hospital.
I have to go to the office.
I have to go to the station.
examples.target: Je dois aller à la gare.

examples.english: I want to buy a ticket.
I want to buy a book.

lessons.title: Today and now
lessons.goal: Attach simple time information without changing the central event
lessons.introduction: Time is an operator on a whole statement. Keep the main sentence shape familiar.

notes.recipe: Subject + finite verb + ... + aujourd’hui/maintenant.
notes.explanation: Time adverbs locate a familiar event without requiring another tense.
notes.detail: Aujourd’hui means today, maintenant means now. The simple guide places these toward the end of the clause.
notes.caution: Other placements are possible in authentic French; our placement is intentionally predictable.

lessons.title: Yesterday: things you did
lessons.goal: Describe completed actions and experiences
lessons.introduction: A useful language needs a real past. Learn one dependable past construction before chasing every literary form.

notes.recipe: J’ai + past participle. / J’avais ... / J’étais ...
notes.explanation: Use passé composé to report a completed action: an auxiliary plus a past participle. Common past states use the imparfait.
notes.detail: J’ai acheté, j’ai travaillé and j’ai compris use avoir. Past possession uses j’avais and past states use j’étais; these are short high-utility imperfect forms.
notes.caution: Passé composé and imparfait express different perspectives. This guide teaches a narrow completed-event versus background-state distinction.

lessons.title: Past journeys and contact
lessons.goal: Say where you went, who you called, and when you arrived
lessons.introduction: Movement verbs may choose a different auxiliary in the past. The shared meaning stays the same.

notes.recipe: Je suis + allé/venu/arrivé/resté.
notes.explanation: Common movement and change-of-state verbs use être in the passé composé.
notes.detail: Je suis allé à la gare, but j’ai appelé. With être, the past participle usually agrees with the subject.
notes.caution: A feminine speaker says allée, venue, arrivée or restée. The generated default masculine form is a starting convention.

examples.target: Je suis allé chez moi hier.

examples.english: I went to the station yesterday.
examples.target: Je suis allé à la gare hier.

examples.english: I went to the hospital yesterday.
examples.target: Je suis allé à l’hôpital hier.

examples.english: I stayed at the hotel last week.
examples.target: Je suis resté à l’hôtel la semaine dernière.

lessons.title: Tomorrow and next week
lessons.goal: Describe upcoming events and near-future plans
lessons.introduction: The goal is to express future meaning, not to memorize a full future-tense paradigm.

notes.recipe: Je vais / vous allez / nous allons + infinitive.
notes.explanation: The futur proche is a simple, natural way to describe an imminent plan. It avoids the full future-tense endings.
notes.detail: Use aller in the present plus an infinitive: je vais travailler demain, nous allons acheter ... demain.
notes.caution: A modal such as pouvoir can stay in the present with a future time word. This keeps the minimal pattern small.

examples.english: I will go to the office tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais aller au bureau demain.

examples.english: I will go to the station tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais aller à la gare demain.

examples.english: I will go to the hotel tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais aller à l’hôtel demain.
Nous allons travailler la semaine prochaine.

examples.english: I will send a message tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais envoyer un message demain.
Je vais envoyer des informations demain.
Est-ce que vous allez venir bientôt ?

lessons.title: Compare past, now, and future
lessons.goal: Reuse the same action across three moments in time
lessons.introduction: These are inflection paradigms generated from one event. Notice what changes and what stays fixed.

notes.recipe: Présent → passé composé → aller + infinitive.
notes.explanation: An event can be viewed as current, completed, or planned by changing one temporal operator.
notes.detail: Compare a conjugated present verb, an auxiliary plus participle, and futur proche. These mechanisms are shared by many verbs.
notes.caution: For ongoing states, French often uses the imparfait instead of passé composé.

examples.english: I will buy a ticket tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais acheter un billet demain.

examples.english: I will buy a book tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais acheter un livre demain.

examples.english: I go to the station today.
examples.target: Je vais à la gare aujourd’hui.

examples.english: I went to the station yesterday.
examples.target: Je suis allé à la gare hier.

examples.english: I will go to the station tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais aller à la gare demain.
Je suis allé chez moi hier.
Je vais aller chez moi demain.

lessons.title: Talk to and about people
lessons.goal: Mention another person, calls, and requests for help
lessons.introduction: The meaning includes both the actor and recipient. The language puts each in the right grammatical form.

notes.recipe: Subject + object pronoun + finite verb.
notes.explanation: French object pronouns normally appear before the finite verb, but before an infinitive after a modal or near-future auxiliary.
notes.detail: Je vous aide, je vous ai aidé, je vais vous aider and je peux vous aider all express the same recipient with a different verb group.
notes.caution: The person receiving help is not automatically a noun after the verb; clitic placement is part of the construction.

lessons.title: Make everyday transactions
lessons.goal: Buy, pay, ask prices, and handle numbers
lessons.introduction: Transactions are composed from needs, quantities, questions, and payment methods.

notes.recipe: Je voudrais ... / deux + plural / Combien coûte ... ?
notes.explanation: Reuse the same small family of nouns, questions and quantities to make many transactions.
notes.detail: One book is un livre; two books is deux livres. To pay by card, use par carte; for cash, en espèces.
notes.caution: The number changes noun morphology and eliminates the singular indefinite article.

examples.english: How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a coffee cost?
How much does a book cost?
How much does a room cost?

examples.target: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
Est-ce que je peux payer en espèces ?

examples.english: I did not buy a ticket yesterday.
examples.target: Je n’ai pas acheté de billet hier.

lessons.title: Describe problems and limits
lessons.goal: Explain illness, lack of time, and things that went wrong
lessons.introduction: Build a fact, then add a cause if needed. Use short separate clauses rather than intricate syntax.

notes.recipe: Je suis malade. Je ne peux pas venir.
notes.explanation: Short statements about a state and an inability are enough to explain a practical problem.
notes.detail: Negate pouvoir with ne ... pas around the finite modal: je ne peux pas travailler. State words may need gender agreement.
notes.caution: Avoid translating a German weil construction word for word. Start with independent clauses.

examples.english: I do not have a problem.
I do not have an appointment.
I cannot come today, because I am sick.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas venir aujourd’hui, parce que je suis malade.

examples.english: I cannot work, because I do not have time.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas travailler, parce que je n’ai pas le temps.

examples.english: I need a ticket, but I do not have money.
examples.target: J’ai besoin d’un billet, mais je n’ai pas d’argent.

lessons.title: Give a reason without hard grammar
lessons.goal: Explain why you cannot do something or need a change
lessons.introduction: Use two simple main clauses linked by “because.” German can use denn rather than a weil subordinate clause.

notes.recipe: Independent clause + parce que + reason.
notes.explanation: The reason can remain a simple subject–verb clause after parce que.
notes.detail: A short cause is sufficient to explain a change of plan. Unlike German, French has no verb-final restructuring here.
notes.caution: Parce que becomes parce qu’ before a vowel: this mini-profile avoids that edge by using simple state reasons.

examples.english: I cannot come, because I am sick.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas venir, parce que je suis malade.

examples.english: I cannot help you, because I am busy.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas vous aider, parce que je suis occupé.

examples.english: I cannot work, because I do not have time.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas travailler, parce que je n’ai pas le temps.

examples.english: I need a ticket, but I do not have money.
examples.target: J’ai besoin d’un billet, mais je n’ai pas d’argent.

examples.english: I cannot go to the office today, because I am busy.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas aller au bureau aujourd’hui, parce que je suis occupé.

examples.english: I worked yesterday, and I will go to the office tomorrow.
examples.target: J’ai travaillé hier, et je vais aller au bureau demain.

lessons.title: Tell a small story
lessons.goal: Report a past event, a present situation, and a next step
lessons.introduction: A short narrative can be three independent simple sentences: yesterday, today, tomorrow.

notes.recipe: Hier ... . Aujourd’hui ... . Demain ... .
notes.explanation: Report a past activity, describe the current situation, and say what you will do next.
notes.detail: Completed event: passé composé. Present situation: présent. Plan: aller + infinitive. Three compact clauses form a useful narrative.
notes.caution: These examples are productive writing models, not an exhaustive treatment of aspect and narration.

examples.english: I went to the hospital yesterday.
examples.target: Je suis allé à l’hôpital hier.

examples.english: I go to the hospital today.
I will go to the hospital tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais aller à l’hôpital demain.

examples.english: I will have an appointment tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais avoir un rendez-vous demain.

lessons.title: Your small communication system
lessons.goal: Combine the core blocks in work, errands, and personal communication
lessons.introduction: Choose a meaning, time, action and possible reason. The same operations produce many new statements.

notes.recipe: Who? + verb + object + time + negation + reason.
notes.explanation: Choose from a limited inventory of meaningful operators. Each operator changes a rule, not a memorized translated phrase.
notes.detail: One core can describe an obligation, a recent purchase, a future call or a reason for being unable to come.
notes.caution: Real conversation also requires understanding varied replies; learning only production is not a full CEFR A2 course.

examples.english: I went to the office yesterday.
examples.target: Je suis allé au bureau hier.
Est-ce que vous pouvez m’aider, s’il vous plaît ?

examples.english: I cannot come, because I am busy.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas venir, parce que je suis occupé.

examples.english: We will buy two tickets tomorrow.
examples.target: Nous allons acheter deux billets demain.

lessons.title: Ask for missing information
lessons.goal: Ask what someone needs, has, or wants and how to get somewhere
lessons.introduction: Open questions are the same event with an unknown slot. Practise the question rule, not a list of shop phrases.

notes.recipe: Qu’est-ce que + subject + verb? / De quoi ... besoin?
notes.explanation: The missing information is one semantic slot. The question word replaces that slot, while the ordinary verb still changes for the speaker.
notes.detail: Qu’est-ce que works for many object questions. Avoir besoin de needs the special question De quoi est-ce que vous avez besoin ? Route questions can start Comment est-ce que…
notes.caution: Question constructions are not identical across languages. Reuse the target language’s question rule rather than translating English word order.

examples.target: De quoi est-ce que vous avez besoin ?
De quoi est-ce que j’ai besoin ?

examples.english: How do I get to the station?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à la gare ?

examples.english: How do I get to the bank?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à la banque ?

examples.english: How do I get to the library?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à la bibliothèque ?

examples.english: How do I get to the hospital?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à l’hôpital ?

lessons.title: Talk about your habits
lessons.goal: Describe how often you study, travel, sleep and work
lessons.introduction: Attach a frequency operator to a present action. The same verb now communicates a routine rather than one event.

notes.recipe: Subject + verb + souvent / parfois + object
notes.explanation: One frequency block can modify many present-tense events: often, sometimes, every day, every week. It describes habitual activity, not an individual finished action.
notes.detail: Short frequency adverbs like souvent usually follow the conjugated verb: Je lis souvent un livre. Every day is tous les jours.
notes.caution: Avoid adding incompatible time operators, such as yesterday and every day, to the same single event.

examples.english: I take a bus every day.
examples.target: Je prends un bus tous les jours.

examples.english: I take a train every day.
examples.target: Je prends un train tous les jours.

lessons.title: Say what you like
lessons.goal: Express simple preferences and react to familiar things
lessons.introduction: Liking is one meaning with different grammar: compare what stays stable and what each language changes.

notes.recipe: J’aime + definite noun / Je n’aime pas + noun
notes.explanation: Expressing a preference is a reusable relation between a person and an object. You do not need a different complete sentence for every food or activity.
notes.detail: With a general preference, use the definite article: J’aime le café; J’aime la musique. Elide je before a vowel: j’aime.
notes.caution: Spanish gustar reverses the typical English logic. The item liked controls the verb, while the person is a recipient.

examples.target: Est-ce que vous aimez le café ?
Est-ce que vous aimez la musique ?

lessons.title: Describe objects and places
lessons.goal: Say whether a thing is good, expensive, open or ready
lessons.introduction: Use a subject and a quality. German uses invariable adjectives here; French and Spanish handle agreement.

notes.recipe: Definite noun + est / était + agreeing adjective
notes.explanation: A description joins an identifiable subject with a quality. This unlocks opinions about housing, prices, condition, and availability.
notes.detail: Adjectives often agree in gender with the noun: le magasin est ouvert, la chambre est ouverte. This guide computes those forms.
notes.caution: Learn which qualities belong to which things. An automatic adjective swap is not always a meaningful sentence.

examples.target: Est-ce que le restaurant est ouvert ?
Est-ce que le restaurant est fermé ?

lessons.title: Talk about housing
lessons.goal: Look for an apartment, describe a room, and ask about availability
lessons.introduction: A housing conversation uses the same operators: need, search, describe, and ask whether something exists.

notes.recipe: Je cherche + logement / L’appartement est + quality
notes.explanation: A practical housing conversation uses search, need, description, and availability. They are productive sentence families, not an apartment vocabulary script.
notes.detail: Chercher takes a direct object. Use the feminine adjective for chambre and the masculine one for appartement.
notes.caution: For detailed leases and legal commitments you will need vocabulary beyond this minimal guide.

examples.target: Est-ce qu’il y a une chambre ?
Est-ce qu’il y a un appartement ?

examples.english: I will reserve a room next week.
examples.target: Je vais réserver une chambre la semaine prochaine.

lessons.title: Find what is nearby
lessons.goal: Ask whether a bank, pharmacy, doctor or other service exists nearby
lessons.introduction: An existence statement is not a memorized location question. Change either the item or its location.

notes.recipe: Est-ce qu’il y a + noun? / Il y a + noun
notes.explanation: Existence and location are different questions. First ask if a service exists; then ask where it is.
notes.detail: The same il y a construction works for nearby services. After negation, un/une usually becomes de: Il n’y a pas de pharmacie.
notes.caution: The most natural location prepositions and articles are language-specific. Learn them with their place names.

examples.target: Est-ce qu’il y a une pharmacie ici ?
Est-ce qu’il y a une banque ici ?
Est-ce qu’il y a un médecin ici ?
Est-ce qu’il y a une bibliothèque ici ?

examples.english: Is there a café at the station?
examples.target: Est-ce qu’il y a un café à la gare ?

examples.english: Is there a shop at the station?
examples.target: Est-ce qu’il y a un magasin à la gare ?

examples.english: Is there a restaurant at the station?
examples.target: Est-ce qu’il y a un restaurant à la gare ?

examples.english: There is a room at the hotel.
examples.target: Il y a une chambre à l’hôtel.

examples.english: There is a restaurant at the hotel.
examples.target: Il y a un restaurant à l’hôtel.

examples.english: There is no bus stop here.
examples.target: Il n’y a pas d’arrêt de bus ici.

lessons.title: Ask the way and get there
lessons.goal: Ask how to reach places and say where you are going
lessons.introduction: Combine a route question with a movement frame. Each language supplies its own preposition.

notes.recipe: Où est + place ? / Comment est-ce que je vais + place ?
notes.explanation: A location question asks where. A route question asks how to get there. Both can be combined with a statement of where you are going.
notes.detail: A destination typically uses à with the appropriate contraction: au parc, à la gare, à l’aéroport.
notes.caution: These patterns ask for directions but do not yet teach you to understand every spoken route explanation.

examples.english: How do I get to the station?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à la gare ?

examples.english: How do I get to the pharmacy?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à la pharmacie ?

examples.english: How do I get to the post office?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à la poste ?

examples.english: How do I get to the city centre?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais au centre-ville ?

examples.english: How do I get to the café?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais au café ?

examples.english: How do I get to the library?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à la bibliothèque ?

examples.english: How do I get to the bus stop?
examples.target: Comment est-ce que je vais à l’arrêt de bus ?

examples.english: I go to the city centre.
We will go to the station tomorrow.
examples.target: Nous allons aller à la gare demain.

examples.english: We will go to the airport tomorrow.
examples.target: Nous allons aller à l’aéroport demain.

lessons.title: Food, cafés and restaurants
lessons.goal: Buy basics, ask about prices and handle a restaurant visit
lessons.introduction: Reuse needs, prices, purchases, and reservations rather than learning a fixed restaurant dialogue.

notes.recipe: Je voudrais + noun / Je réserve + noun
notes.explanation: The same small grammar covers common food purchases, price checks, paying, and booking a table.
notes.detail: Je voudrais is a polite request. Most countable objects need un or une; the grammar uses the noun’s stored gender.
notes.caution: Words like bill and reservation are normal nouns here; they do not exempt a sentence from ordinary articles and word order.

examples.english: I will reserve a table tonight.
examples.target: Je vais réserver une table ce soir.

examples.english: How much does a coffee cost?
How much does a ticket cost?
How much does a room cost?

examples.target: Est-ce que je peux payer par carte ?
Est-ce que je peux payer en espèces ?

lessons.title: Work and education
lessons.goal: Look for work, arrange meetings, and discuss everyday study
lessons.introduction: Introduce a useful job vocabulary through existing past, present, future, and question patterns.

notes.recipe: Je cherche / j’ai + noun; Je travaille tous les jours
notes.explanation: Describe your job, daily routine, email tasks, and future meetings with the same core operators.
notes.detail: Use un emploi for a job and une réunion for a meeting. Je travaille and j’ai travaillé share the same event with a different tense.
notes.caution: Simple workplace communication is not the same as understanding specialist professional or legal language.

examples.english: I will meet a colleague tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais retrouver un collègue demain.

lessons.title: Messages and technology
lessons.goal: Explain what you can open, read, write, send and use
lessons.introduction: Digital communication uses the same verbs and objects as ordinary conversation.

notes.recipe: J’utilise / je lis / j’écris / j’envoie + object
notes.explanation: Use, read, write and send are productive actions. Recombine them with electronic objects and time operators.
notes.detail: Common irregular forms include je lis and j’écris. In a future plan, use je vais écrire + object.
notes.caution: Avoid translating technical terms word for word across countries; each language uses its everyday terms here.

examples.english: I will write an email tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais écrire un courriel demain.

examples.english: I will write a message tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais écrire un message demain.

examples.english: I do not understand the information.
examples.target: Je ne comprends pas les informations.
Est-ce que je peux utiliser un ordinateur ?

lessons.title: Forms and documents
lessons.goal: Ask for documents, complete a form, and explain what you signed
lessons.introduction: Administrative tasks can be communicated with small verb frames and the past operator.

notes.recipe: Je remplis un formulaire / J’ai signé ...
notes.explanation: Paperwork tasks need few new action frames: fill out, sign, read, and send. Attach time and requests as before.
notes.detail: Remplir and signer are direct-object verbs; in the passé composé the past participle follows avoir.
notes.caution: A language guide cannot determine which documents a particular office legally requires.

examples.english: Can you read a document, please?
examples.target: Est-ce que vous pouvez lire un document, s’il vous plaît ?
Est-ce que le document est important ?
Est-ce que le document est prêt ?

examples.english: I will send a document tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais envoyer un document demain.

lessons.title: Health and medicine
lessons.goal: Explain illness and find simple medical assistance
lessons.introduction: Use state + need + destination. Short truthful statements are often easier than complex medical descriptions.

notes.recipe: Je suis malade / J’ai besoin de + noun
notes.explanation: Describe a basic state, request help, and locate medical services using familiar structures.
notes.detail: Use être with malade, and avoir besoin de for needs. The negative of pouvoir is ne peux pas.
notes.caution: The guide does not teach diagnosis, emergency instructions, or how to understand a clinician’s full response.

examples.target: Est-ce qu’il y a un médecin ici ?
Est-ce qu’il y a une pharmacie ici ?

examples.english: I will see a doctor tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais voir un médecin demain.

examples.english: I cannot come, because I am sick.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas venir, parce que je suis malade.

lessons.title: Appointments and services
lessons.goal: Make a plan, ask for help, cancel a meeting and reschedule simply
lessons.introduction: Use short independent sentences to explain a change of plans; do not start with formal subordinate clauses.

notes.recipe: J’ai / j’annule / je vais réserver + noun
notes.explanation: Appointments are nouns. Cancelling, reserving, and explaining a conflict are ordinary verb operators, not special scripts.
notes.detail: Use j’annule for cancellation and je vais réserver for a future reservation. A simple parce que joins a reason.
notes.caution: In many circumstances an earlier or more polite written message is appropriate; short statements are a minimal oral baseline.

examples.english: I will reserve a room next week.
examples.target: Je vais réserver une chambre la semaine prochaine.

examples.english: I will reserve a table next week.
examples.target: Je vais réserver une table la semaine prochaine.

examples.english: I cannot come, because I am busy.
examples.target: Je ne peux pas venir, parce que je suis occupé.

lessons.title: People and social plans
lessons.goal: Say who you will see, whom you are waiting for, and what happened
lessons.introduction: A person can fill a semantic participant or an object slot. Each language handles pronouns and articles differently.

notes.recipe: Je retrouve + person / J’attends + person
notes.explanation: Meeting, calling, and waiting are built from the same participants and objects as other actions.
notes.detail: French attendre takes a direct object without pour. Formal vous works in everyday situations with people you do not know.
notes.caution: Social register varies by region. This guide consistently uses formal second-person forms for unfamiliar people.

examples.english: I will meet a friend tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais retrouver un ami demain.

examples.english: I will meet a colleague tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais retrouver un collègue demain.
Nous l’avons aidé la semaine dernière.

lessons.title: Lost things and problems
lessons.goal: Describe what you lost, what you are looking for, and whether you found it
lessons.introduction: Past + negative + object can communicate most basic lost-property problems.

notes.recipe: J’ai perdu + noun / Je cherche + noun
notes.explanation: Say what happened, what you are looking for, and what you could not find. Reuse the same semantic object in different verbs.
notes.detail: Perdre has past participle perdu. Keep the direct object after the participle; use chercher for the search.
notes.caution: For an official loss report you may need more precise identity details beyond this minimal inventory.

examples.english: I did not find a phone.
examples.target: Je n’ai pas trouvé de téléphone.

examples.english: I did not find a passport.
examples.target: Je n’ai pas trouvé de passeport.

examples.english: I do not have a problem.
I do not have a ticket.

lessons.title: Transport, waiting and delays
lessons.goal: Wait for transport, say when you left, and ask where to go
lessons.introduction: A travel problem is often a short sequence: movement, delay or waiting, next action.

notes.recipe: J’attends un bus / Je suis parti hier
notes.explanation: Use movement, waiting, time, and location. A short description of a delay can be understood without complex syntax.
notes.detail: Movement verbs can take être in passé composé. Partir has parti; with a feminine speaker the participle is partie.
notes.caution: Timetables, platform changes and rapid announcements may still be hard to understand; ask for repetition.

lessons.title: Tell more about the past
lessons.goal: Recount reading, writing, meeting people and losing belongings
lessons.introduction: The past operator does not depend on a particular topic. Change the action, keep the same temporal rule.

notes.recipe: avoir/être + participle; states: imparfait
notes.explanation: Once you know one past construction, many new events become possible without new sentence templates.
notes.detail: J’ai lu, j’ai écrit and je suis revenu share one completed past system. A state such as j’étais fatigué uses imperfect.
notes.caution: Real languages have more than one past tense. MVL teaches a dependable limited contrast, not every narrative nuance.

examples.english: I will read a book tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais lire un livre demain.

examples.english: I will read an email tomorrow.
examples.target: Je vais lire un courriel demain.
Nous avons écrit un message hier.

examples.english: We will write a message tomorrow.

examples.english: I met a friend last month.

examples.english: I saw a doctor last month.
examples.target: J’ai vu un médecin le mois dernier.
Je suis revenu la semaine dernière.

lessons.title: Make fuller plans
lessons.goal: Talk about documents, work and appointments next week or next month
lessons.introduction: Keep the event unchanged; attach the future operator and a time marker.

notes.recipe: aller (present) + infinitive + future time
notes.explanation: Reuse the future operator with different subjects, objects, and time markers to communicate personal plans.
notes.detail: Je vais signer, je vais envoyer, nous allons travailler. The second verb stays in the infinitive.
notes.caution: Plans can change; future meaning in this manual generally assumes an intended event, not a promise or guarantee.

examples.english: I will reserve a table tomorrow.

lessons.title: Connect several simple sentences
lessons.goal: Tell a short personal story with yesterday, today and tomorrow
lessons.introduction: Use two or three complete main clauses in order. You do not need a complex subordinate clause to be understood.

notes.recipe: Hier j’ai/je suis ... . Aujourd’hui ... . Demain je vais ... .
notes.explanation: Two or three independent sentences are enough to give a sequence: what happened, what is happening, and what you will do.
notes.detail: Completed events use passé composé. For future plans use je vais + infinitive. A story can be several very short sentences.
notes.caution: A fluent narrative has richer connections, but this deliberately restricted structure is a reliable starting point.

examples.english: I lost a passport yesterday. I look for a passport. I will go to the bank tomorrow.
examples.target: J’ai perdu un passeport hier. Je cherche un passeport. Je vais aller à la banque demain.

examples.english: I worked yesterday. I am tired. I will sleep tonight.
examples.target: J’ai travaillé hier. Je suis fatigué. Je vais dormir ce soir.

examples.english: I have a meeting today. I will write an email tomorrow.
examples.target: J’ai une réunion aujourd’hui. Je vais écrire un courriel demain.

examples.english: I met a friend last week. We cooked. I will meet a friend next week.
examples.target: J’ai retrouvé un ami la semaine dernière. Nous avons cuisiné. Je vais retrouver un ami la semaine prochaine.

lessons.title: Apply your everyday grammar
lessons.goal: Put needs, time, problems and plans together independently
lessons.introduction: The final unit reuses the same core rules across several different situations. Review weak spots and change the semantic slots yourself.

notes.recipe: Subject + verb + object; add time, question, negation
notes.explanation: Combine the small rules across new topics without rebuilding the sentence from a phrasebook entry.
notes.detail: Notice which parts are reusable and which depend on French: articles, elision, negation, and compound past auxiliaries.
notes.caution: A2-like productive coverage does not guarantee A2 proficiency. You must also practice understanding real speech and written texts.
